background.definition: Eating disorders are complex psychiatric conditions characterized by abnormal eating patterns and a preoccupation with body shape and weight.

list.listitem: Anorexia nervosa (AN): at least 0.08/1000 population per year; incidence rates highest for females between the ages of 15 and 19 years; rates for males estimated to be less than 0.01/1000 population per year (higher in gay and bisexual men), but likely underdiagnosed.
Bulimia nervosa (BN): at least 0.12/1000 population per year; incidence rates highest for females between the ages of 20 and 24 years.
Anorexia nervosa (AN): 9 per 1000 women, 3 per 1000 men.
Bulimia nervosa (BN): 15 per 1000 women, 5 per 1000 men.

Binge eating disorder (BED): 35 per 1000 women, 2 per 1000 men. Authors of a meta-analysis of 39 studies measuring BED, subclinical BED and/or low-frequency of binge eating in children and adolescents found an overall estimated prevalence of 1.32% BED and 3.0% subclinical BED.

In a systematic review of 94 studies published between 2000 and 2018 with accurate ED diagnosis, authors found weighted means (ranges) of global lifetime prevalence of EDs of 8.4% (3.3-18.6%) for women and 2.2% (0.8-6.5%) for men. Point prevalence of EDs was 5.7% (0.9-13.5%) for women and 2.2% (0.2-7.3%) for men and was highest in America compared to Asia and Europe (4.6% [2.0-13.5%], 3.5% [0.6-7.8%] and 2.2% [0.2-13.1%], respectively).

Global prevalence of disordered eating was higher in a more recent meta-analysis of young people with 32 studies including 63,181 participants from 16 countries. In this study, the overall proportion of children and adolescents with disordered eating was 22.4% but studies were quite heterogeneous (95% CI, 18.8%-26.1%, I2 = 98.58%). Girls were significantly more likely to report disordered eating (30%; 95% CI, 25.6%-34.6%) than boys (17%; 95% CI, 13.5%-20.8%).

Similar percentages were reported in a cohort study of 1623 adolescents (829 girls [51.1%]) recruited at a mean age of 14.5 years in which 17.1% reported binge eating and 20.6% reported purging at 14, 16, or 19 years of age.

Authors of a meta-analysis found a peak age of onset of a feeding/eating disorder of 15.5 years (11 studies, median age 18 years, IQR = 15-23). Onset before the ages of 14, 18, and 25 years were 15.8%, 48.1%, 82.4%, respectively.
In one study of 311 high school athletes, 35.4% reported disordered eating, 18.8% reported menstrual dysfunction.

In an Australian study of 531 school boys aged 12 to 18 years, 6.0% of boys reported regular episodes of objective binge eating, 8.3% reported regular episodes of loss of control eating, 5.3% reported regular excessive exercise and 4.9% reported overvaluation of weight or shape.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 36 studies of children and adolescents with overweight and obesity found a prevalence rate of 26.3% (95% CI, 23.1%-29.7%) for binge and loss of control eating.

In an Australian questionnaire study of 715 women aged 40 to 60 years, 33 women (4.6%; 95% CI, 3.3%-6.4%) reported symptoms meeting full DSM-IV criteria for an eating disorder. There were 10 women with BN, 11 women with BED, and 12 with eating disorder not otherwise specified.
In a community-based study of 5658 middle-aged women from the UK, 15.3% (95% CI, 13.5%-17.4%) met criteria for a lifetime eating disorders; twelve-month prevalence was 3.6%.

Among dancers, the overall prevalence of eating disorders is 12.0%. The rate was highest among ballet dancers at 16.4%. The prevalence rate for AN was 2.0% (4% for ballet dancers), 4.4% for BN (2% for ballet dancers), and 9.5% for eating disorders not otherwise specified (14.9% for ballet dancers).

Using the 2012-2013 National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions-III that included 275 subjects with AN, 91 with BN and 256 with BED, prevalence estimates of ever seeking any help for their eating disorder were 34.5%, 62.6%, and 49.0%, respectively. Men and members of ethnic/racial minorities were less likely to seek help.

In a study of 2,118 treatment-seeking adults, the prevalence of BN was significantly lower and the prevalence of BED and other specified feeding or eating disorder was significantly higher among midlife patients vs. younger patients.

In a case series of patients with BED, there was a high prevalence of other psychiatric disorders (eg, mood, anxiety, substance abuse). Based on longitudinal data from Sweden, there was a higher risk of major depressive disorder (OR 7.6; 95 % CI, 6.2-9.3), bipolar disorder (OR 7.5; 95 % CI, 4.8-11.9), anxiety disorders (OR 5.2; 95 % CI, 4.2-6.4), and post-traumatic stress disorder (OR 4.3; 95 % CI, 3.2-5.7) among individuals with BED than age and gender-matched controls.

High rates of future depression (OR 2.9, 95% CI 1.7-5.0) and anxiety (OR 2.5, 95% CI 1.5-4.1) were also reported in a cohort study including 1623 adolescents recruited at a mean age of 14.5 years and followed up at ages 16 and 19 years.
BED is also associated with 28% probability of a comorbid diagnosis of a personality disorder (0.28, 95% CrI 0.22, 0.34), although study heterogeneity in this meta-analysis was high.

Lifetime suicide attempts are also significantly more common in women with all types of eating disorders vs. women with no eating disorder. Authors of a meta-analysis of 52 studies found a prevalence of suicide ideation among patients with eating disorders of 51% (95% CI 41-62%, I2 97.7%) and a prevalence of suicide attempts of 22% (95% CI 18-25%, I2 98.48%).

Rates of non-suicidal self-injury are also increased in patients with AN and BN; authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis reported self-injury rates of 21.8% (95% CI, 18.5%-25.6%) for AN and 32.7% (95% CI, 26.9%-39.1%) for BN.
Female high school athletes reporting disordered eating were twice as likely to be injured compared to those reporting normal eating behaviors (OR 2.3; 95% CI, 1.4-4.0).

Patients with autoimmune and autoinflammatory diseases or a parental history of these disorders appear to be at increased risk for eating disorders. In another study, there was a bidirectional association between AN and celiac disease (prior AN, OR 2.18; 95% CI, 1.45-3.29 for CD and prior CD, OR 1.46; 95% CI 1.08-1.98 for AN).

In 2019, eating disorders were responsible for 6.6 million (3.8-10.6) disability-adjusted life-years (the sum of the number of years lost due to premature death and the number of years lived with a disability).
Loss of gray and white brain matter of 5.6% and 3.8%, respectively, has been reported in patients with AN; following 2 to 8 years of remission, most of the loss is regained.
Eating disorders have a negative impact on family member caregivers, including guilt and distress, and caregivers report many unmet needs.

list.listitem: In one population study, women with AN, BN and BED were more likely to rate their infant’s temperament as extreme fussiness compared to women without these eating disorders (OR 2.3, 1.4, 1.4, respectively). Whether this observation is due to a difference in temperament or information processing bias or other reasons is unknown but additional support to new mother’s with eating disorders should be considered.
Maternal eating disorders are associated with psychiatric diagnosis in their children, particularly emotional disorders (OR 1.9; 95% CI, 1.1-2.8).

In a population-based cohort study in Finland including 392,098 mothers, maternal EDs as well as prepregnancy underweight, and overweight or obesity were associated with most of the studied mental diagnoses in offspring. The largest effect sizes were observed for maternal EDs not otherwise specified in association with offspring sleep disorders (HR 3.3, 95% CI 2.4-4.7]) and social functioning and tic disorders (HR 2.8, 95% CI 2.2-3.5). Maternal EDs were also associated with increased risk of offspring having other feeding disturbances of childhood and infancy (eg, HR 4.5, 95% CI 3.0-6.9) and for maternal AN, there was an increased risk of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and conduct disorder (eg, HR 2.3, 95% CI 1.7-3.0).
Similarly in a Swedish cohort study including 52,878 children, maternal EDs increased risk of ADHD (HRs ranging from 1.4 to 2.0) and autism spectrum disorder (HRs from 2.0 to 2.7).
In one study, children of women with chronic AN had difficulty in social understanding, visual-motor function, planning and abstract reasoning.

Authors of a cross-sectional study of 11,654 pediatric ED hospitalizations between 2002 and 2020 in Ontario Canada, found an increase in hospitalizations for EDs from 2.0 per 10,000 population to 4.8 per 10,000 population. The largest percentage (45.2%) of hospitalizations were for patients with AN, 11.8% were for BN. Over time, increases were greatest for male patients, younger adolescents, and individuals with other EDs by fiscal 2019.

Hospitalizations for ED in the US also increased from pre to post COVID-19 pandemic. ED inpatient volume had been increasing by 1.7 admissions per month pre-COVID, and in the first year post onset, inpatient volume increased by 11.9 per month followed by a 7.6 per month decrease in the second year post onset.
Unknown.

Genetics appear to play a role in AN, with a recent meta-analysis identifying an association between higher risk for AN and tryptophan hydroxylase 2 polymorphism. Authors of a recent genome-wide association study identified one genome-wide significant locus for AN on chromosome 12 (rs4622308) in a region harboring a previously-reported type 1 diabetes and autoimmune disorder locus.

In a study of a large birth cohort in Sweden, AN was independently predicted by multiple birth for twins or triplets vs. singletons and prematurity. BN was predicted by higher birth weight for gestational age.
Life cycle transitional events (e.g., school, job, death of family member) and trauma (illness, abuse, assault) were identified in one small study as triggering events.

Interestingly, mental disorders appear to be transmitted within adolescent peer networks. In a population-based Finnish registry study including 713,809 cohort members born between January 1985 and December 1997 (median age at the start of follow-up of 16.1 years), 6.6% had a mental health diagnosis by 9th grade and 25.1% received a mental disorder diagnosis during follow-up. Investigators found a 5% increase in diagnosis that was greatest for mood, anxiety, and EDs with more than 1 diagnosed classmate (HR 1.05; 95% CI 1.04-1.06). The highest risk occurred during the first year of follow-up; there was a 9% increase for 1 diagnosed classmate (HR, 1.09; 95% CI, 1.04-1.14) and an 18% increase for more than 1 diagnosed classmate (HR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.13-1.24).
Complex combination of biological, genetic, psychological, environmental, and social factors.

In a longitudinal cohort study including 1623 adolescents recruited at mean age 14.5 years and reassessed at ages 16 and 19 years, high levels of neuroticism (OR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.06), conduct problems (OR 1.4, 95% CI 1.2-1.7), and deliberate self-harm (OR 2.2, 95% CI 1.4-3.4) were associated with future binge eating. Deliberate self-harm (OR 2.6, 95% CI 1.7-4.0), conduct problems (OR 1.4, 95% CI 1.2-1.7), alcohol misuse (OR 1.3, 95% CI 1.1-1.5), and drug abuse (OR 2.9, 95% CI 1.8-4.7) were associated with future purging. Perfectionism (r = 0.25), perfectionistic strivings (r = 0.21), and perfectionistic concerns (r = 0.31) also had significant positive associations with ED symptoms in another meta-analysis.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 62 studies found social physique anxiety largely related to EDs (r = .51). In a meta-analysis of 195 studies, shame was significantly associated with a medium to large effect size with all types of eating disorders symptoms (r’s between .40 and .52) with body shame (r = .55) and shame around eating (r = .59) being more strongly related with ED pathology.

The unique contribution of any specific factor remains unclear. Serotonin neuronal systems are implicated and a recent Spanish study purports to be the first to demonstrate an association between 5-HT3 variants and AN.
People with AN have impaired osmoregulation that is likely multifactorial in etiology.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 21 functional neuroimaging studies found a significant hyperactivation cluster in the right putamen and a significant hypoactivation cluster in the left inferior parietal lobule in participants with disordered eating compared to controls. This suggests potential pathophysiological mechanisms underlying anticipatory responses to rewarding and aversive cues in ED.
The role of gut microbiome in contributing to poor weight gain and neuropsychiatric abnormalities is under study, with significant effects noted in studies on mice.

list.listitem: Preteens and adolescents should be asked about eating patterns and satisfaction with body appearance as part of routine wellness care. C

However, the United States Preventive Services Task Force found insufficient evidence to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for eating disorders (EDs) in adolescents and adults (age 10 years and older) who have no signs or symptoms of EDs.
The SCOFF questionnaire () can be used as a self-report instrument for screening. B
Based on a systematic review of prevention of eating disorders, effective preventive strategies include media literacy, CBT, a healthy-weight program, and psychoeducation. B

The SCOFF questionnaire has been validated using a primary care population sample; in this setting, the questionnaire had a sensitivity of 84.6%, a specificity of 89.6%, and detected all true cases of AN and BN and 7 of 9 cases of eating disorder not otherwise specified. Similar sensitivity (86%, 95%CI 78-91%) and specificity (83%, 95% CI 77-88%) for SCOFF was reported in a meta-analysis of 25 screening studies.

Self Administrated Psychiatric Scales for Children and Adolescents (SAFA) is a potential screening test for eating disorders in children. A subscale of the SAFA (SAFA P [psychogenic eating disorders]) was recently found to be reliable for assessing EDs compared to the Eating Disorder Inventory-2.

The United States Preventive Services Task Force (2022) found insufficient evidence to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for EDs in adolescents and adults (age 10 years and older) who have no signs or symptoms of EDs (eg, rapid weight loss, weight gain, or pronounced deviation from growth trajectory, pubertal delay, bradycardia, oligomenorrhea, and amenorrhea).
The American Medical Society for Sports Medicine (2020) recommends routine annual preparticipation screening for athletes, by consensus opinion.

In a study of 94 adolescents with obesity, the Adolescent Binge Eating Scale questionnaire was useful in identifying those at high risk of BED. In another study of 70 patients aged 7 to 18 years attending a pediatric obesity program of whom 34% met full diagnostic interview criteria for BED, the Children's Brief Binge-Eating Questionnaire demonstrated 100% specificity, 93% sensitivity, and a 100% negative predictive value for BED using a cutoff total score of 9.

Authors of a systematic review of prevention of EDs identified media literacy as having the most support for universal prevention and dissonance-based therapy for selective prevention efforts; other effective selective prevention strategies included CBT, a healthy weight program, media literacy, and psychoeducation. Use of prevention programs for EDs is supported by the American Medical Society for Sports Medicine (2020).

School-based programs, including combinations of nutrition education, criticism of aesthetic models of beauty emphasizing extreme thinness, and media literacy, appear to improve nutrition knowledge and eating attitudes among Spanish adolescents.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 27 intervention studies conducted at universities found a 38% decrease in incidence of developing a subthreshold or full-blown ED in the intervention groups compared to controls (RR 0.62, 95% CI 0.4-0.9, NNT = 26). In another meta-analysis that also found a reduced risk of EDs from preventive interventions, intervention techniques used in the 23 studies included were cognitive dissonance; CBT; multi-component, media literacy; psychoeducation; physical activity; and medication.

In another meta-analysis of 15 trials involving 5080 participants (mean ages ranging from 14.5 to 22.3 years), authors found that healthy lifestyle modification prevention programs and dissonance-based prevention programs were most successful (OR 1.6, 95% CI 1.1-2.45), with prevention effects being significantly larger for trials that recruited participants with elevations on a single risk factor vs. those with multiple risk factors. In this study, interventions using psychoeducation, CBT, behavioral weight gain, interpersonal and family-therapy did not significantly reduce future onset of EDs.

Self-help programs appeared less successful based on 7 studies in which there was a significant but very small effect (pooled g = -0.17) of interventions at post-treatment which was non-significant at follow-up.
As “fat talk”—self-deprecation and negative comments about one’s weight—is associated with body dissatisfaction, limiting fat talk may be helpful.
Patients identified during an initial screening or evaluation as having a possible ED should undergo an in-depth interview and a physical examination before a diagnosis is made. C
Family members should be involved during the assessment of pediatric and adolescent patients. C
No laboratory test is diagnostic for an ED; the need for testing should be determined on an individual basis. C

Diagnosis.Diagnostic_criteria:
DSM-V-TR criteria are:
Anoreia Nervosa (AN): At a significantly low body weight for their developmental stage (guidance for this determination is available in the text of DSM-V); intense fear of weight gain or becoming fat; disturbance in the way one's weight or body shape is experienced; undue influence of body weight/shape on self-evaluation or denial of seriousness of low body weight. Specific types include restricting and binge-eating/purging. Bulimia Nervosa (BN): Recurrent episodes of binge eating (at least 1 time per week for 3 months) described as eating in a discrete period more than what most people would eat during that time with an associated perceived lack of control during a binge; recurrent inappropriate compensatory behavior(s) occurring on at least 1 time per week for 3 months; body shape and weight significantly affect self-evaluation. Specific types include purging and nonpurging. Eating disorder not otherwise specified: Diagnosis used for individuals who do not meet the criteria for a specific eating disorder. Includes BED (recurrent episodes of binge eating without compensatory behaviors). The proposed International Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD)-11 diagnostic guidelines had significantly improved accuracy relative to ICD-10 for all EDs tested using vignettes presented to 2288 mental health professionals registered with WHO's Global Clinical Practice Network.

list.listitem: Consider eating disorders in the following groups: young woman with a low BMI when compared with age norms; patients who express concern about weight but who are not overweight; women with menstrual disturbances or amenorrhea; patients with GI symptoms, physical signs of starvation, and/or repeated vomiting; and children with poor growth.

Patients will typically present with nonspecific complaints including: fatigue, dizziness, low energy, amenorrhea, weight loss, constipation, bloating, abdominal discomfort, gastroesophageal reflux, sore throat, palpitations, polyuria, polydipsia, and/or insomnia. Family members are likely to express more concern about symptoms than the patient.

Authors of a review paper noted that individuals with EDs are disproportionately represented among people seeking care for gastrointestinal symptoms, in particular, functional gastrointestinal disorders.

Dental problems are more common among patients with EDs. In a small matched case-control study of 54 outpatients with EDrs, patients with EDs were more likely to present with dental problems (OR 4.1), burning tongue (OR 14.2), dry/cracked lips (OR 9.6) and dental erosion (OR 8.5) than healthy controls.

Patients with AN describe an intense fear of weight gain and pursue weight loss (through severe calorie restriction and/or excessive exercise/purging behaviors) despite being at or below 85% of their ideal body weight, as defined by age-appropriate body mass charts.
Patients with BN will report a preoccupation with weight and a pattern of dieting, binge eating, and purging behaviors.
The Ravello Profile test battery is under investigation for use in assessing neuropsychological profiles specific to AN.

The American Psychiatric Association (APA) 2023 guideline recommends assessment of vital signs, including temperature, resting heart rate, blood pressure, orthostatic pulse, and orthostatic blood pressure; height, weight, and BMI (or percent median BMI, BMI percentile, or BMI Z-score for children and adolescents); and physical appearance, including signs of malnutrition or purging behaviors.

Physical examination may be normal. Findings suggestive of an eating disorder include: lanugo, Russell's sign (calluses on dorsum of hand), bradycardia, orthostatic hypotension, hypothermia, peripheral edema, dental caries with dental enamel erosion, parotid gland swelling, epigastric tenderness, abdominal swelling, atrophic breast or vaginal tissue, delay or arrested sexual development, ecchymosis, anxious/depressed mood, delayed skeletal growth, bony point tenderness, and loss of muscle mass.

The Society for Adolescent Health and Medicine recommends measurement of percent median body mass index, BMI Z-scores, and amount and rate of weight loss to assess severity of malnutrition in adolescents with EDs.

No test is diagnostic. Recommended tests for the evaluation of a patient with a suspected or confirmed ED include: a CBC, UA, liver function tests, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, glucose, and TSH. The APA also recommends a complete blood count and a comprehensive metabolic panel, including electrolytes, liver enzymes, and renal function tests for those suspected with an ED. The purpose of these tests is to screen for complications of the disorder and to rule out alternative diagnoses.
Elevated liver enzymes were present in 37% of 356 subjects 10 to 22 years of age with AN who were admitted to a tertiary children's hospital.

Possible associated laboratory abnormalities include: hypoglycemia, euthyroid sick syndrome (low TSH, normal T3 and T4 levels), hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatemia, increased urine specific gravity, increased BUN concentration, decreased serum creatinine, normocytic normochromic anemia, mild leukopenia with related lymphocytosis, and thrombocytopenia.
Patients with amenorrhea may need additional testing to include: urine pregnancy test, prolactin, estradiol, luteinizing hormone, and follicle-stimulating hormone.

An ECG should be performed in any patient with bradycardia or electrolyte abnormalities. The APA 2023 guidelines also recommend an ECG for patients with a restrictive eating disorder, patients with severe purging behavior, and patients who are taking medications that are known to prolong QTc intervals.
A clinical decision rule with 5 questions can predict the likelihood of an eating disorder, from 1.5% in the lowest risk group to 14.5% in the highest risk group.

Consider eating disorders in young women with a low BMI compared with age norms; patients who express concern about weight but who are not overweight; women with menstrual disturbances or amenorrhea; patients with GI symptoms, physical signs of starvation, and/or repeated vomiting; and children with poor growth.

Questionnaires such as the Eating Disorder Examination, the Eating Disorder Examination-Self-Report Questionnaire (EDE-Q; English and Spanish versions) and the Body Esteem Scale can be useful in identifying cases of ED. For patients with BED, a factor of the Bulimia Test-Revised (called the Binge Eating Disorder Test or BEDT) and the Eating Concern subscale of the EDE-Q, were shown in one study to have high sensitivity (100 vs. 87), specificity (96 vs. 100), positive predictive values (94 vs. 100), and negative predictive values (100 vs. 93), respectively.

The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends that the initial evaluation includes establishing the diagnosis, evaluating medical and nutritional status, determining severity, and performing an initial psychosocial evaluation.
Questionnaires such as the Rating of Eating Disorder Severity Interview for Children can be useful in determining severity of an eating disorder.

The APA guideline (2023) recommends assessment for co-occurring health conditions and psychiatric disorders (e.g., mood, anxiety, substance use disorders, and suicidality). Depression preceding AN is associated with decreased likelihood of recovery.Depression is also a contributor to negative self-esteem in AN and body dysmorphic disorder.

Order a CBC, calcium, magnesium, glucose, liver function tests, electrolytes, TSH, and UA. Order ECG if patient has bradycardia or electrolyte abnormalities. Additional tests may be indicated in patients with amenorrhea (as noted above). An erythrocyte-sedimentation rate, screening for celiac disease, or radiographic imaging may be considered if there is diagnostic uncertainty.
See for an algorithm to help determine the most appropriate treatment setting.

Primary care clinicians can assist patients and their families in selecting high calorie foods without increasing food volume, supplementing for deficiencies (e.g., iron), and establishing expectations for weight and sports participation while a patient is waiting for specialty treatment.

The Society for Adolescent Health and Medicine endorses higher calories and more rapid increase than the historical standard of care. They suggest determination of treatment goal weight for an individual should be based on previous height, weight and BMI percentiles, pubertal stage, and growth trajectory. The total weight goal should be reassessed every 3–6 months.
Pretreatment motivation to change is associated with a change in restrictive eating and bingeing behaviors, and with cognitive/affective measures of eating disorder pathology.

Intensive treatment (inpatient, residential and day program) appears to result in significant improvements in BMI for underweight patients, disordered eating, depression, and quality of life based on a meta-analysis of 62 studies.

Compulsory treatment is sometimes needed for patients with EDs. Authors of a meta-analysis including 242 compulsorily and 738 voluntarily treated patients found mean illness duration, BMI at discharge and BMI variation were not significantly different between the two groups, although average length of hospitalization was 3 weeks longer among compulsory-treated patients.

Treatment is ideally provided by an interdisciplinary team that, at a minimum, includes a primary care physician, behavioral health provider, and a dietitian—all of whom should be familiar with treating eating disorders.

The Society for Adolescent Health and Medicine notes that weight restoration is an important early treatment goal and treatment should be individualized with consideration of premorbid trajectories for height, weight, and BMI; age at pubertal onset; and current sexual maturity. B
Psychotherapies should be used as first-line treatment in patients with eating disorders. If employed, drug therapy is typically used in combination with psychotherapies.

Most patients with AN should be treated on an outpatient basis by a multidisciplinary team that can provide psychotherapies as well as physical monitoring of symptoms. APA 2023 guidelines recommend individualized goals set for weekly weight gain and target weight for patients with AN who require nutritional rehabilitation and weight restoration and disorder-focused psychotherapy. They recommend eating disorder-focused family-based treatment for adolescents and emerging adults with AN.
CBT and/or interpersonal therapy should be provided to patients with BN and BED.
The American Medical Society for Sports Medicine (2020) recommends CBT and family therapy as treatments for EDs in athletes. B

A trial of an antidepressant medication may be offered as an alternative primary therapy or as an additional treatment for BN and BED. For patients with BN, APA 2023 guidelines recommend combination eating disorder-focused CBT or family-based treatment for adolescents and emerging adults with BN who have an involved caregiver and a serotonin reuptake inhibitor (e.g., 60 mg fluoxetine daily), either prescribed initially or if there is minimal or no response to psychotherapy alone by 6 weeks of treatment. C
Lisdexamfetamine (a central nervous system stimulant) and topiramate can also be considered for patients with BED.
Psychotropic medications are of limited efficacy in the treatment of AN and should only be used as adjuvant agents when treating comorbid disorders.

In one randomized cross-over 4-week trial of 25 women with AN of at least 5 years duration, dronabinol, a synthetic cannabinoid agonist, was more effective than placebo in positive weight change. No severe adverse effects were noted.

Olanzapine, an atypical antipsychotic, increased BMI over placebo (0.259 [SD=0.051] vs. 0.095 [SD=0.053] per month, respectively) but there were no differences in psychological symptoms between groups in an RCT of 152 adult patients with AN. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 studies (AN = 9, BN = 10, BED = 3) confirmed olanzapine benefit for increasing BMI in AN over placebo but not fluoxetine. Small sample sizes and short trial duration limit conclusions.
Low-dose testosterone therapy was not effective for weight gain or improvement in symptoms for women with AN.

Authors of a systematic review of 12 RCTs found good evidence supporting the efficacy of antidepressants in the treatment of BN. Antidepressants decrease the frequency of episodes of binge eating and purging with associated improvements in mood. The combination of CBT and antidepressant therapy has added benefit over medication or behavioral therapy alone.
Authors of the meta-analysis noted in the previous section found fluoxetine reduced binging and purging episodes in BN but did not significantly change weight.

SSRIs (e.g., fluoxetine 60 mg daily) are recommended as first-line agents because of their efficacy and safety profile. Despite its efficacy, bupropion is contraindicated because of the association of its use with seizures in patients who purge.

Authors of a systematic review of 8 medication-only RCTs (including SSRIs, tricyclic antidepressants, antiepileptics, and appetite suppressants) concluded benefit for short-term treatment of BED. The addition of antidepressant medication to CBT does not appear to improve efficacy. Placebo response was reported as 38% and cessation in 26% in a pooled analysis of 10 clinical trials of BED from one research group.

In the most recent meta-analysis of 25 placebo-controlled trials that evaluated pharmacologic (n = 19) or combination (n = 6) treatment, lisdexamfetamine, topiramate, and second-generation antidepressants decreased binge-eating frequency and increased binge-eating abstinence; lisdexamfetamine and topiramate also reduced weight. Side effects of lisdexamfetamine include headache, gastrointestinal upset, sleep disturbance, and sympathetic nervous system arousal.
In a study of topiramate, the drug was effective for BED but poorly tolerated.

An RCT comparing CBT plus placebo with CBT plus orlistat demonstrated greater remission rates and greater initial weight loss in individuals treated with CBT plus orlistat. In another RCT, sibutramine was more effective than placebo in reducing the number of binges per week (2 vs. 3) and reducing weight (7.4 kg loss vs. 1.4 kg gain for placebo).

In two multicenter RCTs, lisdexamfetamine was more effective than placebo in decreasing binge eating days/week (study 1: −1.35 [−1.70, −1.01]; study 2: −1.66 [−2.04, −1.28]) and improving binge eating-related key secondary endpoints. Side effects included dry mouth, insomnia, and headache.

In another RCT of patients with BED, 275 of 418 (66%) lisdexamfetamine responders by 12 weeks (defined as ≤1 binge eating day per week for 4 consecutive weeks) were randomized to continued drug treatment vs. placebo. Lisdexamfetamine significantly reduced risk of binge-eating relapse over 6 months (3.7% vs. 32.1%, respectively).

In a 16-week, 4-arm RCT including 136 patients with BED comorbid with obesity comparing combination naltrexone-bupropion plus behavioral weight loss (BWL) therapy, either intervention alone or placebo, BWL was significantly superior to no BWL and naltrexone-bupropion was significantly superior to placebo for binge-eating remission. Remission rates were 57.1% for naltrexone-bupropion plus BWL, 31.3% in the naltrexone-bupropion group, 37.1% in the BWL+placebo group and 17.7% in the placebo group. There was no significant interaction between BWL and medication for remission. BWL was significantly superior to no BWL for achieving 5% weight loss which occurred in 38.2% in the BWL+naltrexone-bupropion group, 31.4% in the BWL+placebo group, 18.8% in the naltrexone-bupropion group, and 11.8% in the placebo group. BWL was also superior to no BWL for improvements in secondary measures (eating disorder psychopathology, depression, eating behaviors, and cholesterol and HbA1c levels).

Treatment is ideally provided by an interdisciplinary team that includes, at a minimum, a primary care physician, behavioral health provider, and a dietitian—all of whom should be familiar with treating eating disorders.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 54 RCTs including 5463 patients across a range of mental health and somatic disorders, including 5 trials on body image or eating disorders, found moderate-certainty evidence of little to no difference in the effectiveness of in-person compared to therapist-guided remote CBT.

Nutritional rehabilitation is considered in markedly underweight children and adolescents. With respect to target goals, expected rates of controlled weight gain are 2 to 3 pounds (lb)/week for hospitalized patients and 0.5 to 1.0 lb/week for individuals in outpatient programs often achieved through a structured meal plan, expanding food choices, and possibly formula feeding.

In an RCT of two refeeding strategies in 36 adolescents with AN, refeeding at 1200 kcal/d vs. 500 kcal/d resulted in greater weight gain at 10 days (−1.2% median body mass index; 95% CI, −2.4%-0.0%) but had no influence on other outcomes or complication rates. (see other treatment below)

Patients with AN should be offered some form of psychotherapy (eg, CBT, interpersonal, cognitive analytic, focal dynamic, or family intervention) as first-line treatment, although the efficacy of these measures is unclear.

In an RCT of focal psychodynamic therapy, enhanced CBT, or optimized treatment as usual in 242 patients with AN, there was positive weight change in all patient groups at treatment end and at 12 months (1.64, 1.30, and 1.22 kg/m2, respectively) with no significant differences between groups. There was a high dropout rate of 30% at 12 months.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 10 trials of individual psychological therapy with 599 patients with AN were unable to draw conclusions compared to usual care due to risk of bias and small sample sizes.

In one study of 32 patients with AN who had achieved some weight restoration, use of Exposure and Response Prevention compared favorable to Cognitive Remediation Therapy (CRT) in improving intake and eating-associated anxiety. CRT, which focuses on enhancing cognitive flexibility, a neurocognitive trait marker in AN, has been shown to be effective in performance of cognitive set-shifting. Drop out from treatment was high at 15/40 patients (37.5%).

Family-based therapy is recommended by the Society for Adolescent Health and Medicine as first-line outpatient psychological treatment for adolescents with AN. Family therapy may be effective in the short term compared to treatment as usual based on limited evidence from two trials; evidence is insufficient to determine whether family therapy approaches are superior to educational interventions based on a Cochrane review.

In one RCT of 164 adolescents with AN, family-based therapy focused on the facilitation of weight gain was comparable to systemic family therapy (which addressed general family processes) for remission rates (about 40%), eating disorder symptoms, and comorbid psychiatric disorders at end-of-treatment and follow-up, but was associated with lower costs ($8963 vs. $18 005, respectively).

In another RCT of family-based therapy provided to 169 adolescents with AN or unspecified eating disorder, randomization to multi-family therapy was more effective than single-family therapy in achieving a good or intermediate outcome (based on the Morgan-Russell scales) at the end of treatment (75% vs. 60%, respectively). At 18-month follow-up, there was little change compared to end of treatment but the difference in outcome between treatments was no longer statistically significant.

A small body of evidence supports treatment of BN with CBT (16-20 sessions). In one RCT of 70 patients with BN, there was a large difference observed in cessation of binge eating and purging for patients randomized to CBT vs. psychoanalytic psychotherapy (42% vs. 6%). Significant differences remained at 2 years (44% vs. 15%; OR 4.34; 95% CI, 1.33-14.21). Additional psychotherapies that may be efficacious include interpersonal therapy and self-help approaches.

As noted above, in a 4-arm RCT, behavioral weight loss (BWL) therapy was significantly superior to no BWL for binge-eating remission and resulted in greater weight loss for patients with BED and obesity.

Authors of a systematic review of 26 studies found moderate evidence supporting the use of CBT for treatment. Evidence-based self-help programs and interpersonal therapies were also effective. Counseling on weight loss may also need to be provided. Schema therapy and appetite-focused CBT are suitable alternative treatments to traditional CBT for BED.

In an RCT of 178 patients randomized to internet-based guided self-help vs. traditional, individual face-to-face CBT, those randomized to traditional CBT had fewer binge-eating episodes and greater reductions in eating disorder psychopathologic findings.

However, internet-based CBT also reduced frequency of binge episodes and improved some pathological features related to eating in patients with BED compared to control patients based on a meta-analysis of 11 RCTs. Authors reported heterogeneity across studies, some limitations of self-assessment scales, and potential publication bias.

Dialectical therapy, a form of therapy that combines CBT techniques for emotion regulation with concepts of distress tolerance, acceptance, and mindful awareness largely derived from Buddhist meditative practice, may be effective for patients with EDs, but findings are mostly based on uncontrolled studies.
Mentoring for patients with eating disorders and disordered eating has qualitative value for both mentors and mentees.
Dietary counseling should be considered for all patients with EDs, but should not be the only treatment.

A nutritional rehabilitation program should be established for all underweight patients with a short-term goal of 0.5 to 1.0 kg weight gain per week and a long-term goal of an age-appropriate and sex-appropriate weight.

There is little evidence supporting optimal methods for refeeding for weight restoration in hospitalized children and adolescents (aged 19 years and younger) with AN. Tube feeding led to greater interim or discharge weight but was associated with a higher incidence of adverse effects.

In a recent RCT including 111 patients with AN, higher-calorie refeeding with 2000 kcal/d and increasing by 200 kcal/d restored medical stability significantly earlier than lower-calorie refeeding consisting of 1400 kcal/d and increasing by 200 kcal every other day (HR 1.7, 95% CI 1.1-2.5). Electrolyte abnormalities and other adverse events did not differ by group and hospital stay was 4.0 days shorter (95% CI -6.1 to -1.9 days) among the group receiving higher-calorie refeeding.
Neuromodulation procedures of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation and deep brain stimulation have led to symptom reduction in patients with AN and BN.
For patients with severe and enduring AN, palliative and hospice care may be offered along with comfort and support in alignment with the patient’s wishes.
For patients with AN, psychotherapeutic treatment typically lasts for at least 1 year after weight restoration. Treatment may continue for many years.
In individuals assigned female sex at birth, resumption of spontaneous menses can help guide achievement of treatment goal weight.

Medical indications for hospitalization for patients with AN include: heart rate less than 50 bpm during daytime or less than 40 bpm at nighttime, blood pressure less than 90/60, symptomatic hypoglycemia, potassium less than 3 mmol/L, temperature less than 36.1°C or 97.0°F, dehydration, other cardiovascular abnormalities, weight less than 75% of the expected weight, body fat less than 10%, refusal to eat, rapid weight loss, or lack of improvement while in outpatient therapy.

Indications for hospitalization for patients with BN include: syncope, serum potassium concentration less than 3.2 mmol/L, serum chloride concentration less than 88 mmol/L, esophageal tears, cardiac arrhythmias including prolonged QTc, hypothermia, suicide risk, intractable vomiting, hematemesis, and failure to respond to outpatient treatment.

Psychological indications for possible hospitalization: poor motivation/insight, lack of cooperation with outpatient treatment, inability to eat, need for nasogastric feeding, suicidal intent or plan, severe coexisting psychiatric disease, or problematic family environment. Most patients struggling with EDs can be treated as outpatients.

Osteoporosis may occur in patients with an eating disorder. A dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan is recommended, particularly in patients with amenorrhea for longer than 6 months. The primary treatment is weight gain.

In a meta-analysis of 57 studies, individuals with AN compared to healthy controls had reduced BMD, increased odds of osteoporosis (OR 12.59; 95% CI, 3.30-47.9) and increased risk of fractures (OR 1.84; 95% CI, 1.17-2.89).

In one longitudinal study of 80 women with AN, thirteen subjects (16%) had a low spinal BMD at baseline. Ten incident asymptomatic vertebral fractures identified on DEXA imaging occurred in 9 subjects (12.5%) at 18 months; only 2 subjects had more than 15% loss in vertebral height.
Bisphosphonates are not recommended because of concerns about efficacy and long-term safety.

Teriparatide (human PTH[1-34]) administration was shown in one RCT to increase spine BMD after only 6 months of therapy in women with AN; influence on fractures is unknown. Reduced BMD may be persistent.

An RCT of 94 women with AN found combination dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) + a combined oral contraceptive (COC) superior to placebo in preserving skeletal health (as measured by spinal and whole-body bone mineral density z scores) over 18 months. It is not known whether this combination is superior to COC alone.

Irreversible dental erosions may occur in patients who purge. Patient should be instructed to use a baking soda mouth rinse and to brush teeth after vomiting, in addition to routine dental care. Desensitizing toothpaste and fluoride application may decrease tooth sensitivity.

In a population-based cohort study in Ontario including 6139 people aged 13 years or older with an ED and an outpatient electrolyte measure within 1 year, 1987 (32.4%) had an electrolyte abnormality. The most common abnormalities were hypokalemia (50%), hyponatremia (37.8%), and hypernatremia (21.1%).

Refeeding syndrome is a metabolic complication that is potentially life-threatening and occurs as metabolism shifts from a catabolic to an anabolic state with release of insulin on carbohydrate intake, triggering cellular uptake of potassium, phosphate, and magnesium. The incidence of RFS varied widely from 0% to 62% across 35 studies and refeeding hypophosphatemia occured in between 7% and 62%.

The rise in aminotransferases seen in patients with AN is caused by hepatocyte injury and death from starvation. Malnutrition-induced hepatitis is common among individuals with AN, especially with more extreme weight loss, and acute liver failure associated with coagulopathy and encephalopathy can rarely occur.

For patients with severe AN requiring surgery, one author recommends nutritional support until surgery and cautions against careless loading of glucose or catecholamine as this can lead to electrolyte disturbance or fatal arrhythmia.
Patients hospitalized because of an unstable medical status should be monitored closely for refeeding syndrome (described above).

Caution should be exercised during early refeeding for patients with low admission prealbumin levels. In one study, these patients had a threefold increased risk of refeeding hypophosphatemia and a twofold increase of hypoglycemia vs. patients who had a normal admission prealbumin, independent of BMI.

As part of the follow-up care of patients with eating disorders, periodic physical examinations and laboratory evaluations should be performed to evaluate for medical complications. C Electrolyte abnormalities are associated with higher complication rates. B
Following treatment, patients with BN and BED are more likely to achieve remission than patients with AN. C
Disordered eating behaviors decrease over time. B

Electrolyte abnormalities occur in many patients with eating disorders. Among the 32.4% with electrolyte abnormalities in the Canadian population study of 6163 patients with eating disorders cited above, investigators found higher hospitalization rates (60.5% vs. 47.4% for those without electrolyte abnormalities) and mortality rates (15.7% vs. 5.6% in those without electrolyte abnormalities; absolute risk difference 10.1%; adjusted HR 1.2, 95% CI 1.03-1.5). There were also higher rates of acute kidney injury (10.4% vs. 3%; HR 1.91, 95% CI 1.5-2.4), chronic kidney disease (12.3% vs. 4.3%; HR 1.4, 95% CI 1.2-1.8), bone fracture (7.0% vs. 4.0%; HR 1.4, 95% CI 1.1-1.8), and bowel obstruction (3.6% vs. 1.4%; HR 1.6, 95% CI 1.1-2.4).
Authors of a meta-analysis of 16 studies of EDs found that relapse occurred in 24.5% and EDs persisted into early adulthood in 40.7% of cases.

Following treatment in a tertiary care setting, approximately 70% of individuals with BN and 30% to 50% of those with AN will not show evidence of a clinical eating disorder within 10 years. In one 3-year follow-up study of 43 patients with bulimia (84% of total), one-third of patients showed complete remission, one-third showed partial remission, and one-third still fulfilled all the criteria of BN.

Following treatment, 40% to 87% of patients with BED no longer binge after treatment. In one 4-year follow-up of patients with BED who had participated in a RCT, there was substantial long-term recovery with partial remission, stable body mass index, and significant reductions in associated psychopathology despite relapse episodes. Those participating in group interpersonal psychotherapy fared better than those participating in group CBT with respect to symptoms at follow-up.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 17 studies found reductions in restrictive eating and other compensatory behaviors over time with risk reductions of between 20-40% for 10-year follow-up and 25-75% for ≥15-year follow-up.
Rapid response to treatment predicts better cognitive and behavioral outcomes.
Higher level of care, having psychiatric comorbidity, and higher severity of ED psychopathology are associated with relapse, based on a meta-analysis of 35 papers.

Long-term outcome is worse in patients with AN than BN and includes a higher risk of mortality, including death from suicide. Vomiting, bulimia and purgative abuse, chronicity, and obsessive-compulsive features are unfavorable prognostic factors.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 36 studies reported weighted disease-specific mortality rates (i.e., deaths per 1000 person-years) of 5.1 for AN (1 in 5 deaths caused by suicide), 1.7 for BN, and 3.3 for nonspecific eating disorders.

Among 818 women hospitalized for BN in Quebec and followed for up to 12 years, women with BN had 4.25 (95% CI, 2.98-6.07) times the risk of any cardiovascular disease and 4.72 (95% CI, 2.05-10.84) times the risk of death compared with women hospitalized for pregnancy-related events; this included a higher risk of ischemic heart disease (HR, 6.63; 95% CI, 3.34-13.13) and cardiac conduction defects (HR, 2.99; 95% CI, 1.57-5.71).

Prevalence of lifetime obesity was 28.8% in a follow-up study of 1383 patients with EDs who were admitted between 2001 and 2010 to a University Hospital (ranging from 5% in patients with AN to 87% in patients with BED).

Although there does not appear to be a significant difference in cancer incidence in women with at least one hospitalization for AN compared to women in the general population, there was a higher mortality from cancer in one study, specifically from melanoma, genital organ cancers, and cancers of ill-defined, secondary and unspecified sites.
After the initial evaluation, a physical examination and laboratory evaluation should be performed periodically to evaluate for medical complications.

Outcomes to consider in follow up include eating disorder behaviors and cognitions, physical health, co-occurring mental health conditions, and quality of life and social functioning. The International Consortium for Health Outcomes Measurement suggest use of the following measurement tools based on age: For children aged 6 to 12 years, potential measures include the Children's Eating Attitude Test (or, for those with avoidant restrictive food intake disorder, the Eating Disorder in Youth Questionnaire), the KIDSCREEN-10, and the Revised Children's Anxiety and Depression Screener-25. For adolescents aged between 13 and 17 years, potential measures include the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q; or, for avoidant restrictive food intake disorder, the Nine-Item Avoidant Restrictive Food Intake Disorder Screener [NIAS]), the two-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-2), the nine-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9), the two-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-2), the seven-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD-7), and the KIDSCREEN-10. For adults older than 18 years, measures include the EDE-Q (or, for avoidant restrictive food intake disorder, the NIAS), the PHQ-2, the PHQ-9, the GAD-2, the GAD-7, the Clinical Impairment Assessment, and the 12-item WHO Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0.
Fluoxetine (up to 60 mg/day) may help prevent relapse; however, adding fluoxetine to CBT after weight restoration does not appear to confer additional benefit.

An RCT of an internet-based relapse prevention program for 258 women with AN conducted over 9 months appeared effective in increasing weight (vs. minimal weight loss for control women) and in a more favorable course for "sexual anxieties" and "bulimic symptoms" (based on interview), and "maturity fears" and "social insecurity" (based on EDI-2).

In an RCT of 172 adolescents with non-chronic AN, day treatment after short inpatient care was as effective as inpatient treatment for weight restoration and maintenance during the first year after admission.
Patients and family members should be educated on the nature, course, and treatment of EDs.
Family members and caregivers of children and adolescents with EDs should be given guidance on behavioral management strategies such as meal planning and limit-setting.
Family member participation in support groups should be encouraged.
Late-onset anorexia nervosa (>50 years old) may be a long-term disease or may represent a new illness triggered by the death of loved one, marital discord, or divorce.

The global prevalence of EDs among pregnant women was 4.3% (95% CI 2%-9%; I2 = 99.5%) with a range of 0.5 to 10.6%, based on a systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 studies involving 2,369,520 pregnant women.
Pregnant women with EDs should be monitored closely throughout the pregnancy and postpartum to ensure they are providing adequate nutrition for themselves and their fetus.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis including 18 studies found positive associations between AN and low birth weight (OR 1.7, 95% CI 1.5-2.0), AN and small for gestational age infants (OR 1.4, 95% CI 1.2-1.6), BN and preterm birth (OR 1.2, 95% CI 1.04-1.4), and BED and large for gestational age infants (OR 1.4, 95% CI 1.2-1.7). EDs were not significantly associated with miscarriage.

In a database study from Helsinki University Central Hospital, women with AN treated at the Eating Disorder Clinic compared to unexposed women had a higher risk of delivering infants with a lower birthweight, very premature birth, small for gestational age, low birthweight, and perinatal death. Women with BN had a higher risk of neonatal resuscitation and very low Apgar score at 1 minute and women with BED had a higher risk of maternal hypertension, long labor, and birth of large-for-gestational-age infants compared to unexposed women.

In a Swedish population-based cohort study of all singleton births from 2003-2014, including 7542 women with EDs, risks were increased for women with EDs for hyperemesis (RR 2.1-2.6), preterm birth (RR 1.3-1.6), and delivering neonates with microcephaly (RR 1.4-1.9).
In a large cohort study, adverse perinatal events were not seen in women with EDs controlling for other factors; smoking was more prevalent among these women.
Children often present with nausea, abdominal pain or fullness, and the inability to swallow.

Adolescent males are most often diagnosed with "eating disorder not otherwise specified," and frequently display poor emotional wellbeing and low family and/or school connectedness. The number of same-sex partners is greater than for unaffected peers. Participation in low-weight-oriented sports (eg, runners, wrestlers, jockeys) is associated with increased risk of disordered eating.

Additional indications for hospitalization in children include: heart rate less than 50 bpm, orthostatic blood pressure, hypokalemia or hypophosphatemia, and rapid weight loss even if weight is not less than 75% of the expected normal weight.

feature.caption: The SCOFF Questionnaire for Eating Disorders.
feature.feature_body: A patient responding "yes" to 2 or more questions suggests a likely diagnosis of anorexia nervosa (100% sensitivity, 87% specificity, LR+ 7.6, LR− 0.13). Do you make your self-sick because you feel uncomfortably full? Do you worry you have lost control over how much you eat? Have you recently lost more than 1 stone (14 lb/6.7 kg) in a 3-month period? Do you believe yourself to be fat when others say you are too thin? Would you say that food dominates your life? From Morgan JF, Reid F, Lacey JH. The SCOFF questionnaire: assessment of a new screening tool for eating disorders. BMJ 1999;319:1467-1468.
